transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, thank you for fitting me in. I, uh... I really didn't know who else to talk to about this. I'm a tax preparer, you see, so my whole life is built around things being very grounded, very logical. Numbers on a page, clear rules, everything exactly where it should be. I've been doing this for decades, ever since I got my bachelor's, and my office is practically my second home. 

But lately... well, what brings me in today is that I keep having these incredibly bizarre moments. It's hard to even explain without sounding crazy, but it's like my own house, or even my office, suddenly feels completely unreal. I'll just be sitting there, maybe looking at a client's return, and all of a sudden it's like... like I'm watching myself from across the room instead of actually being there in my own chair. Like I'm hovering over by the filing cabinets, just observing this man working. I can see my hands typing or holding a pen, but they don't quite feel like my hands, and the room itself looks like a cheap stage set or a photograph instead of a real, physical place. 

It just washes over me, this profound sense of being disconnected from my own life, and it takes me a good while to shake it off. I've tried drinking more coffee, getting up and walking around, but nothing really stops it from happening. I just can't keep working or living like I'm a ghost haunting my own desk, you know? It's just so deeply unsettling to feel like a spectator in your own life.
How often do these feelings happen, and do they come on suddenly or build up over time?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that because, being a tax preparer, my whole life is about tracking things, right? I mean, if a client asks me how often they can claim a certain business expense, I have the exact frequency, the exact parameters right there in front of me. I'm a data guy. But with this... I honestly couldn't give you a hard number. I really don't know. 

I haven't been keeping a log, which frankly bothers me more than I care to admit. Sometimes I think to myself, "Okay, I'll write it down the exact minute the next time it happens," but then I'm in that weird, floaty state and I completely lose my train of thought. So, how often? I'm not sure. More than I'd like, obviously, but I couldn't say if it's a specific amount of times a week or... or what. 

And as for how they come on... well, I've tried to analyze that too, to see if there's a pattern. I'll sit there afterward and try to retrace my steps. Like, was I looking at a particularly complicated schedule C? Was the fluorescent lighting in my office acting up? Did I feel it creeping up on me while I was getting my morning coffee? But... I just don't know. I can't really pinpoint a build-up, but I also can't say for sure it's like a light switch, you know? It's just... I'm working, I'm doing my normal routine, the exact same routine I've had since I was fresh out of college with my bachelor's, and then suddenly I'm just... noticing that I'm in it. I wish I could give you a better timeline or a clear cause-and-effect, doctor, I really do. It's incredibly frustrating for me not to have the exact data to hand over to you.
When you feel disconnected like this, does it ever feel like your body isn't yours, or that the world around you isn't real?

Well, yes and no. I mean, it's... it's a very difficult thing to articulate precisely, and as I mentioned, I'm usually very good at being precise. But when it happens, the feeling about my body... it's not that I look down at my hands and think they belong to someone else, like some stranger walked in and swapped arms with me. It's more like... like they are my hands, I recognize the wedding band, I recognize the little scar on my left knuckle from when I was ten and fell off my bike, but they just feel... hollow? Or maybe mechanical is a better word. Like I'm operating a machine that happens to look exactly like my body. I'll be holding a pen, right? A standard blue ballpoint, nothing special, and I know my fingers are gripping it, I can see the ink going onto the paper, but the sensation of holding it feels miles away, like it's being reported to me on a time delay. 

And as for the world around me... that's where it gets really strange. It doesn't disappear, it doesn't turn into a cartoon or anything completely absurd, but it loses its... its depth, I suppose. I was sitting in my living room the other night, just trying to watch the evening news, the same news I watch every night at 6:30, and suddenly the television, the coffee table, the curtains my wife picked out five years ago... they all just looked flat. Like a really high-definition photograph of my living room, rather than the actual room itself. Or like a stage set, where you know if you knock on the wall it'll just be cheap plywood. It's all there, exactly where it's supposed to be, every book on the shelf in its proper place, but the essence of it being real, solid matter just vanishes. It's incredibly disorienting, doctor. I try to blink it away, I try to focus really hard on the texture of the couch upholstery to ground myself, but it's like there's this invisible pane of glass between me and the rest of the universe. So, yes, it feels unreal, but not because it changes shape or anything. It's just... the reality gets drained right out of it.
Do these feelings of unreality in the world around you happen separately from the times you feel disconnected from your body, or do they tend to happen together?

You know, it's... well, it's exactly like I was trying to explain when I first came in today, when I was telling you what brought me here in the first place. It's really both at once. The moments where my own house or my office suddenly feels completely unreal—like that flat, fake stage set I was talking about—those are the exact same times I feel like I'm watching myself from across the room instead of actually being there in my chair. 

It’s a package deal, unfortunately, which is just... it’s so incredibly disruptive to my workflow and my life. I’ll be trying to focus on a client's W-2, just a standard form I've looked at thousands of times since I got my bachelor's, and it's not like the room goes flat on Tuesday and then I feel disconnected from my body on Thursday. No, it's all at once. The walls start looking like cheap plywood, the depth just drains right out of the room, and simultaneously, I'm suddenly... I'm over by the doorway, or hovering near the filing cabinets, just observing this 54-year-old tax preparer going through the motions. 

I can see myself sitting there at the mahogany desk, but I'm not *in* myself, and the place I'm sitting in doesn't feel like a real physical space anymore. I've actually sat there afterward and tried to analyze it, to see if one triggers the other—like, does the room fade first, and then I pop out of my body? Or do I detach first, and then the room changes? Because if I could figure out the sequence, maybe I could stop it. But honestly, doctor, I can't separate them. They just hit me together, this overwhelming wave of... of just not being present, in a place that doesn't even feel real either. It makes it nearly impossible to get any actual work done when you're dealing with both of those things simultaneously, you know? I just want things to be solid and logical again.
Have you ever experienced the sense of the world feeling unreal without also feeling detached from your body, or vice versa?

Well, no, like I was just trying to explain a moment ago, they really don't ever happen independently of one another. I've never experienced one without the other, which, as an analytical person, is incredibly frustrating because you always want to isolate the variables, right? If a client has a tax discrepancy, you look for the single point of failure. You don't just throw your hands up. But with this, I can't separate them. 

It always comes back to exactly what brings me in to see you today: I just keep having these moments where my own house or my office feels entirely unreal, and concurrently, it's exactly like I'm watching myself from across the room instead of actually being there in my chair. 

I've never had a situation where I'm sitting at my desk and the office feels like a fake movie set, but I still feel like I'm solidly inside my own body. And I've never had a time where I'm floating over by the filing cabinets watching myself work, but the room itself still looks totally normal and real. It's always both. Every single time. I've racked my brain trying to think of even one instance—maybe late at night when I'm tired, or early in the morning before my coffee—where only one of those things happened, just to give you a better data point, but I can't. It's always that exact same combined experience. The unreality of the space and the... the watching myself from a distance. They are completely, one-hundred-percent linked together for me.
Have these episodes ever occurred when you were not under any particular stress or during a calm, routine moment?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because you would think—logically, right?—that a person would only experience something so bizarre during a high-stakes situation. Tax season, for instance. April 14th, phones ringing off the hook, clients panicking about their deductions, a complicated audit... that would make sense. But no, it's actually quite the opposite sometimes. It happens during the most mundane, tranquil moments you can imagine. 

I know I keep hammering on this exact same point, and I apologize if I sound like a broken record, but I really have to emphasize that what brings me in here to see you is that I just keep having these moments where my own house, or my office, feels completely unreal, and it's like I'm watching myself from across the room instead of actually being there. And it happens when absolutely nothing stressful is going on! 

Just last Sunday, for example. The house was dead quiet. My wife was out at the grocery store, I was just sitting in my recliner with a cup of decaf coffee—decaf, mind you, so it wasn't even a caffeine jitter—just looking out the front window at the lawn. No deadlines, no complicated tax codes to decipher, no stress whatsoever. Just a perfectly calm, routine Sunday morning. And then, out of nowhere... boom. The living room turns into that flat stage set again. The reality just drains out of the walls, and suddenly I'm floating over by the staircase, looking at myself sitting in the recliner holding the coffee mug. 

So, yes, it doesn't seem to require any sort of panic or immediate stress to trigger it. It just invades these perfectly quiet, routine moments, which honestly makes it even more disturbing. If it only happened when I was overwhelmed at work, I could just manage my workload better, right? I could delegate. But if I can't even sit in my own house on a Sunday morning without the room turning fake and feeling like I've been ejected from my own body... well, how am I supposed to plan for that? It defies all logic.
Have you ever experienced these feelings of unreality or detachment when you were not also experiencing any other emotional or psychological symptoms, like anxiety, depression, or intrusive thoughts?

Well, that's... that's a very interesting question, doctor, because you'd think there would be some sort of emotional buildup, right? Like, you'd think I'd be sitting there stewing in anxiety or feeling deeply depressed about something, or maybe obsessing over some mistake on a client's return. But honestly, no. And I know I've said this exact same thing about three times now—and I really do apologize for circling back to it yet again—but it always just comes down to what brought me in here in the first place: I just keep having these moments where my own house or my office suddenly feels completely unreal, and I feel like I'm watching myself from across the room instead of actually being there. 

And the thing is, it happens even when my mind is completely clear. Like I mentioned with that Sunday morning... I wasn't anxious. I wasn't depressed. I didn't have any intrusive thoughts about work or my marriage or my health or anything else. My mind was just... quiet. Neutral. I was just a guy drinking decaf and looking at his lawn. And yet, there it was again. The walls go flat, the room loses all its depth, and suddenly I'm hovering by the stairs watching myself sit there. 

It's so frustrating because, as a tax preparer, I'm trained to look for cause and effect. If there's a penalty on a return, there's a reason—a missed deadline, an underpayment, a mathematical error. There's always a preceding event that explains the outcome. But with this... there's no emotional trigger that I can pinpoint. I'm not having a panic attack, I'm not spiraling into some dark depression, I'm not obsessing over anything. I'm just sitting there, perfectly fine, and then bam—my office or my living room turns into a movie set and I'm ejected from my own body. 

It's completely illogical, which is why I'm here talking to you, because I just can't make sense of it on my own. I've tried to analyze it from every angle, looking for some hidden anxiety or some subconscious thought that might be kicking it off, but I always come up empty. It just happens, totally independently of any other emotional state.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent episodes of depersonalization and derealization occurring concurrently, without evidence of another emotional or psychological state triggering them. The symptoms are consistent with depersonalization-derealization disorder (F44.2), and do not meet criteria for other specified dissociative disorder (F44.8) given the consistent and specific nature of the experiences described.
